catalog_quote: [Vossen 2003: 181-182, §1] Stress is said to exist but, according to Heine, its "exact significance is unclear." ... stress appears to play a certain role in the formation of finite verbs. Heine (1999: 18) cautiously states: "Typically it is found on the last high tone syllable preceded by a low tone within the same word." My own data, however, seem to suggest that stress as a distinctive unit is inherent even to the citation form of the verb. This article is strictly empirical-descriptive. It confines itself to the treatment of verbal tone and stress ... sweep_summary: ǁAni is not in the catalog. Both sweep items are the same work, Vossen 2003 'Verbal tone and stress in ǁAni' (FAB 15:181-191), which is the only first-hand treatment of ǁAni stress; no open copy exists (Köppe print; HathiTrust/Frankfurt/De Gruyter routes blocked), but Google Books feed snippets now yield section 5 almost verbatim: stress sits on the last H-toned syllable of the verb stem for tone classes 2/3/5 and shifts to the juncture morpheme for classes 1/4, with the intro quoting Heine 1999:18 ('last high tone syllable preceded by a low tone within the same word'). Downing 2010 (paywalled, p. 394) summarises this as 'last High-toned syllable of verbs' with exceptions; Downing 2004 (open, read) predates it and has nothing on ǁAni. Heine 1999 (Khoisan Forum 11) remains print-only. A catalog entry would be coded from Vossen 2003 as tone-conditioned, verb-only stress (last H syllable of stem, or juncture); acquiring the full Vossen article (and Heine 1999) is the high-priority gap.

new_statements.rule_in_words: ǁAni is a (mora-based) tone language; in addition, verbs carry a stress whose position is tied to tone: it falls on the last High-toned syllable of the word (Heine: the last H syllable preceded by a L within the word). Vossen argues stress is a distinctive property already of the verb's citation form (he marks it lexically per verb stem in an appendix), and Downing notes Vossen reports exceptions to the last-H generalisation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: Downing 2010 fn.: 'See Vossen (2003) for detailed discussion of ǁAni, including some exceptions to the pattern mentioned here.' Vossen: homophonous citation forms can differ in finite shapes; stress treated as distinctive (lexical) in verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about verbs (citation forms and finite verb forms incl. juncture/TAM suffixes); nominal stress not treated by Vossen 2003 ('confines itself to the treatment of verbal tone and stress'). Word-level, tone-conditioned.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern ǁAni proper (anii1246; Vossen's fieldwork on the upper Okavango, Ngamiland; Heine 1999 same variety). Fehn 2019 treats ǁAni as a variety of the Khwe dialect cluster (Khwe = kxoe1243, separate languoid); Kilian-Hatz 2008 describes West Caprivi Khwe, not ǁAni. Fehn's open Ts'ixa grammar describes Ts'ixa (own Glottolog languoid, though 'Ts'éxa' appears among Glottolog's //Ani alt names) and was not used for the statement.

new_statements.quote: Besides tone, stress appears to play an important role in the formation of finite verbs. In most cases it is acoustically perceptible. To verbs of tone classes 2, 3 and 5 stress is inherent in the sense that the accent is retained on the verbal stem throughout, be it simple, derived, reduplicated or composed. In each case the stress-bearing unit is the last H-tone syllable. [...] verbs of tone classes 1 and 4 are observed to shift stress to the juncture morpheme.
new_statements.citation: Vossen, Rainer (2003 [2004]). Verbal tone and stress in ǁAni (Central Khoisan). In R.-J. Anyanwu (ed.), Stress and Tone – the African Experience (Frankfurter Afrikanistische Blätter 15), 181-191. Köln: Köppe.
new_statements.locator: section 5 'The interaction of tone and stress', pp. 185-186
new_statements.reading: ǁAni verbs carry a tone-dependent stress: in tone classes 2, 3 and 5 the stress stays on the last high-toned syllable of the verb stem in all forms; in tone classes 1 and 4 it moves to the juncture (tense) morpheme in finite forms, so stress placement is lexically conditioned by tone class and morphologically conditioned by the juncture, not a fixed edge-based rule. Nouns are not treated. Caveat: assembled from overlapping snippet views, not from a full copy; the passage boundaries are exact but a few words between 'listed in (9)' and 'verbs of tone classes 1 and 4' are missing.

sources.note: Stress is a verb-level property tied to tone: for verbs of tone classes 2, 3 and 5 ([+stress] in the appendix lists) the accent sits on the last H-toned syllable of the verbal stem in every form; for tone classes 1 and 4 ([-stress]) the stress shifts onto the juncture morpheme in finite forms, giving prosodic minimal pairs between otherwise homonymous verbs (ts'óó 'rot' vs. ts'óó with juncture stress).
